theme: Restore us, O God, the vine brought out of Egypt
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 80. It is a prayer of the northern tribes for restoration, and its image of the vine echoes Isaiah 5. Notice the refrain that returns three times, each time with a fuller name for God.
settingTheScene: Psalm 80 is a psalm of Asaph set to the tune “Lilies, a Testimony.” It names the northern tribes Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh, and so was probably written around the fall of the northern kingdom. It is placed here to answer Isaiah’s vineyard song. Isaiah says the vineyard produced wild grapes. The psalmist asks the vinedresser to come back and tend it.
observation: “Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel, you who lead Joseph like a flock” (v. 1).
“Restore us, O God; let your face shine, that we may be saved!” (v. 3).
“O LORD God of hosts, how long will you be angry with your people’s prayers?” (v. 4).
“You have fed them with the bread of tears and given them tears to drink in full measure” (v. 5).
“You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it” (v. 8).
“Why then have you broken down its walls, so that all who pass along the way pluck its fruit?” (v. 12).
“Turn again, O God of hosts! Look down from heaven, and see; have regard for this vine” (v. 14).
“But let your hand be on the man of your right hand, the son of man whom you have made strong for yourself!” (v. 17).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with the image of a shepherd and moves to the image of a vine. In both, God is the caretaker of his people. The psalmist reminds him of what he did: he brought a vine out of Egypt, cleared the ground, and let it take root until it filled the land. The vine reached from the mountains to the sea. Then the walls fell, and the vine was burned and cut down. This is Isaiah 5 from the other side. Isaiah says the vine did not bear fruit. The psalmist pleads that God would not abandon it.

The refrain is the heart of the prayer. It appears three times, with the name of God growing. “Restore us, O God” (v. 3). “Restore us, O God of hosts” (v. 7). “Restore us, O LORD God of hosts” (v. 19). Each time the same request: “Let your face shine, that we may be saved.” As the prayer deepens, the psalmist uses a fuller and more covenantal name. It is the language of someone who is coming closer to God as they pray.

Notice that the psalmist does not ask for the nation to reform itself. He asks God to restore. The people cannot fix their own spiritual condition. “Let your face shine” is the old priestly blessing of Numbers 6. Salvation is the shining of God’s face.

Verse 17 introduces a mysterious figure: “the man of your right hand, the son of man whom you have made strong.” Perhaps this is the king, or Israel as God’s son. But the language points beyond them. The vine needs a representative who will do what the vine failed to do. The psalm ends with a vow: “Then we shall not turn back from you; give us life, and we will call upon your name.” Renewal produces faithfulness.
connection: Jesus said, “I am the true vine” (John 15:1), the faithful Israel who bears fruit and in whom we are branches. “The son of man at God’s right hand” is a title Jesus used of himself (Mark 14:62; Daniel 7:13). Hebrews 1:3 says he sits at the right hand of the Majesty. 2 Corinthians 4:6 says God has shone in our hearts “to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.”
application:
Pray the refrain “Restore us, O God; let your face shine, that we may be saved” for yourself and for your church.

Think about an area of your life that has been “broken down.” Ask God to restore it.

Thank God that the true vine, Jesus, bears all the fruit that Israel did not.
prayerPrompts: Ask the Shepherd of Israel to restore you where you are ruined.
Ask him to let his face shine on you.
Thank him for the man at his right hand.
